title: Tonsils and adenoids: immune tissue in the throat
intro: Tonsils are part of the immune system near the entrance to the airways and digestive tract. They help recognize germs, particularly during childhood, but do not form a perfect barrier. A sore throat does not always mean the tonsils need antibiotics or surgery.

sections.heading: Different locations
paragraphs: The palatine tonsils are visible at the back of the mouth. Adenoids lie higher behind the nose and cannot normally be seen by looking into the mouth. Other related immune tissue is found near the tongue.

sections.heading: Immune activity
paragraphs: Immune cells sample material and help develop responses to infections. Tissue size changes with age and infection. Large tonsils alone do not prove severe disease, while smaller ones can still become inflamed.

sections.heading: Infection and obstruction
paragraphs: Viruses and bacteria can cause inflammation, but appearance alone cannot always distinguish them. Enlarged tissue may also affect swallowing or breathing during sleep. Persistent snoring with pauses or daytime effects deserves assessment.

sections.heading: Treatment decisions
paragraphs: Care depends on severity, cause, repeated episodes and breathing effects. Antibiotics help selected bacterial illness, not every sore throat. Surgery has potential benefits and risks, including bleeding and recovery pain; removal does not remove all immune defenses.

sections.heading: Urgent symptoms
paragraphs: Difficulty breathing, drooling with inability to swallow, marked one-sided swelling, a muffled voice or trouble opening the mouth needs urgent assessment. Bleeding after tonsil surgery is urgent even if it seems to settle. Do not delay because an earlier sore throat was mild. Before a consultation, note when a symptom began, what makes it better or worse, and how it affects ordinary activities. Bring previous reports if available. Ask the professional to connect the explanation to your own findings rather than assuming that a general description establishes a diagnosis.

examples.title: A practical example
examples.text: In this hypothetical example, Mira records repeated infections and their effect on school before discussing options, rather than requesting surgery after one ordinary episode.

examples.title: Another practical example
examples.text: In this hypothetical example, Arben notices a child snoring with breathing pauses. He seeks assessment for obstruction instead of assuming snoring is always harmless.
